records.title: MCPExternalSync removes only the ids an older build recorded, from three third-party files, once ever
records.expected_result: Return immediately unless <data root>/mcp/managed.json exists - nothing in this source ever writes that file, so on a fresh install this is a complete no-op. When it exists, read it as {"cursor": [ids], "opencode": [ids], "gemini": [ids]}, defaulting each to an empty list, and remove those ids from: ~/.cursor/mcp.json under root key "mcpServers"; ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json under root key "mcp"; ~/.gemini/settings.json under root key "mcpServers". Then DELETE managed.json, so it can fire at most once ever. remove skips an empty id list, a missing file, unparseable JSON or a missing root object; it removes exactly the listed ids, leaves every other key alone, and rewrites the file atomically with pretty-printed sorted-keys JSON only when something was actually removed. The servers parameter is never referenced in the body.
side_effects: may rewrite up to three third-party configuration files in the user's home directory
failure_cases: every failure mode is a silent skip that leaves the file untouched
records.windows_path: Not ported: NOT_APPLICABLE_WITH_EVIDENCE under ED-061 (see not_applicable). exportAll omits the call (PR-MCP-082). Upstream's intent, kept for the record: clean an upgrading user's %USERPROFILE%\.cursor\mcp.json, %USERPROFILE%\.config\opencode\opencode.json and %USERPROFILE%\.gemini\settings.json once; no build of the app ever wrote managed.json on Windows, so there is nothing to clean.
records.verification_method: static check: the Windows tree has no MCPExternalSync equivalent, exportAll makes no such call (PR-MCP-082), and nothing reads, writes or deletes mcp\managed.json
records.not_applicable: ED-061: porting/dead_code.md entry 11 ([mcp] MCPExternalSync in its entirety, MCPExternalSync.swift:1-64). sync() returns at :9 unless mcp/managed.json exists, and nothing in the pinned source writes managed.json (every managedURL reference is the :52 declaration, the :9 existence check, the :27 removeItem and the :55 read; rechecked at B2 by grep for "managed" and "MCPExternalSync" over the Swift tree). The file could only come from an older Droppy Code build, which is macOS only, and no build that runs on Windows writes it, so the migration never executes: it is neither implemented nor counted as missing.

records.title: The in-app hub lists tools per server, caching successes and blacklisting servers whose listing failed
records.preconditions: An in-app model-API provider is assembling its tool list.
records.expected_result: Specs are read from claude.json on first use and cached until reload. Server ids are iterated in sorted order. A server with a cached tool list contributes it without any network or process work. A server in the failed set is skipped entirely. Otherwise a client is created or reused, listTools is awaited, and on success the list is cached and appended. On failure the line "MCPHub: <id>: <message>" is printed, the id is added to the failed set and the client is stopped. The whole result is sorted by server id, then by tool name.
side_effects: may launch one child process or open one HTTP session per server
one unconditional console line per failure
failure_cases: a failing server is silently absent from the model's tool list
records.cancellation: awaiting tools() is a cancellation point; a cancelled listTools is treated as a failure and blacklists the server
records.windows_path: Same ordering and caching. The sort is observable because it fixes the order tools are presented to the model.
records.verification_method: integration test with one good and one failing stand-in server

records.title: A tool call name is mcp__ plus the server id, two underscores, and the tool name
records.action: A tool is exposed to a model, or a model's call is routed.
records.expected_result: callName = "mcp__" + server + "__" + name. parse requires the "mcp__" prefix, then finds the FIRST occurrence of "__" in the remainder: the text before it is the server and the text after it is the tool, and both must be non-empty or the parse fails. So a server id containing a double underscore would split at the wrong place; no catalog id or makeID-minted id contains one, but a tool name containing "__" is safe because only the first separator is used.
failure_cases: an unparseable name throws MCPHubError.unknownTool(name) -> "Unknown tool: <name>."
records.windows_path: Same grammar; it is the contract between the model, the transcript renderer and the hub.
records.verification_method: unit with a tool name containing a double underscore

records.title: A tool call is rejected only when its server is unknown or its name is absent from a cached list
records.preconditions: A model emitted a tool call.
records.expected_result: Specs are loaded if needed. An unparseable call name, or one naming a server with no spec, throws unknownTool. When a cached tool list exists for that server AND does not contain the tool, throw unknownTool. When no cache entry exists the check is SKIPPED, so a server whose listing failed is relaunched by a direct call - call() never consults the failed set. The client is created or reused and callTool is awaited. An MCPHubError is rethrown unchanged; a CancellationError is rethrown as a fresh CancellationError; anything else becomes MCPHubError.server(error.localizedDescription).
side_effects: may launch a child process for a server that previously failed to list
failure_cases: "Unknown tool: <name>." for both rejection cases
the server's own message for anything else
records.cancellation: cancellation propagates as CancellationError, not as a server error
records.windows_path: Reproduce the asymmetry exactly: do not add a failed-set check to call(). A listing failure hides the server from the tool list yet a direct call still relaunches it.
records.verification_method: integration test calling a tool on a server whose listing failed

records.title: reload drops every client, cache and failure and stops the running processes asynchronously
records.expected_result: The current client map is captured, then clients, the tool cache, the failed set and the specs are all cleared, so the next tools() or call() re-reads claude.json from disk. Each captured client is stopped in its own detached task, so reload returns immediately and the terminations happen in the background.
side_effects: terminates every running in-app MCP child process
failure_cases: none
records.windows_path: Same: clear first, stop asynchronously. A synchronous stop would block the settings interaction that triggered the export.
records.verification_method: integration test asserting a toggled-off server's process ends and the next call re-reads the file

records.title: The hub reads its server specs from claude.json, preferring a command over a url
records.expected_result: Read <data root>/mcp/claude.json; a missing, unparseable file or a missing mcpServers object yields an empty map, so the hub exposes no tools. For each member: when "command" is a non-empty string, the spec is stdio with that command, the string elements of "args" and the string-valued pairs of "env"; otherwise, when "url" is a non-empty string, the spec is http with that url and the string-valued pairs of "headers". A member with neither is skipped. Non-string values inside args, env and headers are dropped silently.
failure_cases: a deleted claude.json means the in-app providers get no MCP tools at all
records.windows_path: Same precedence and the same silent dropping of non-string values.
records.verification_method: unit over both branches and a member with neither key

records.title: The hub's tool listing caps descriptions at 400 characters and substitutes an empty object schema
source_evidence: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:36-51 listTools, the ten-page cursor loop the hub shares with the probe
records.expected_result: At most 10 pages of tools/list, each with a 60-second timeout, carrying a cursor only when one was returned. For each tool: a name is required or the item is skipped; the description is the raw description or the empty string, truncated to its first 400 characters; the schema is the item's inputSchema when it is an object, otherwise the literal {"type": "object", "properties": {}}. Pagination stops when nextCursor is absent or empty. Unlike the probe, the hub keeps the truncated description rather than a first line.
side_effects: up to ten requests per server
records.persistence: none; the hub's cache is in memory only
failure_cases: an error at any page propagates and blacklists the server in tools()
records.cancellation: each request is a cancellation point
records.windows_path: Same 400-character cap and the same schema fallback: they are what the model sees.
records.verification_method: unit with an over-long description and a tool with no inputSchema

records.title: A tool result is flattened to text lines with placeholders for images and resources
records.preconditions: A tool call is being made.
records.expected_result: A null arguments value becomes an empty object. The request is tools/call with params {"name": <tool>, "arguments": <args>} and a 120-second timeout. From result.content, in order: an item with a string "text" contributes that text; an item whose "type" is "image" contributes the literal "[image]"; an item whose "type" is "resource" contributes "[resource: <resource.uri or the empty string>]"; anything else contributes nothing. The lines are joined with a single newline. isError is result.isError when it is a boolean, otherwise false.
side_effects: one tool call on the server
failure_cases: an error reply throws MCPHubError.server(message)
records.cancellation: the request is a cancellation point
records.windows_path: Same flattening and the same two placeholder strings, which appear verbatim in the transcript.
records.verification_method: unit over text, image, resource and unknown content items

records.title: A hub stdio client restarts at most once and is then permanently dead
records.expected_result: A client already marked dead throws server("The server quit.") without trying. A running, initialized process is reused. Otherwise, when a stdio connection already exists: if a restart was already used, mark the client dead and throw server("The server quit."); else record that a restart is being used. Then start the process. So each client gets exactly one relaunch for the whole life of the hub's client map, and only a reload clears it.
failure_cases: "The server quit." once the single restart is spent
records.windows_path: Scope the restart policy to stdio only; the HTTP path has no restart and no dead state at all.
records.verification_method: integration test killing a stand-in server twice

records.title: A hub stdio client launches with the login environment, registers for quit-time termination, and handshakes with a 60-second initialize
source_evidence: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPHub.swift:279-306 startStdio - :288 connection = try MCPStdioConnection.launch(executable: executable, arguments: args, environment: environment) | :290 throw MCPHubError.server(error.localizedDescription) | :293 MCPHub.track(connection.process) | :295 let reply = try await stdioReply(connection, method: "initialize", params: MCPWire.initializeParams(), timeout: 60) | :299 connection.notify("notifications/initialized")
DroppyCode/Core/Support/StdioProcess.swift:55-88 start - stderr is appended to the bounded buffer; when the launch fails both handlers are detached and the message stream is finished
records.preconditions: A stdio spec that must be started.
records.expected_result: An unresolvable command throws server("<command> isn't installed."). The environment is the login environment with the spec's env layered on; the working directory is the user's home. The child is launched as an MCPStdioConnection: stdout is framed into messages (PR-MCP-112) and stderr is kept in the process's bounded buffer, which the hub never reads. A launch failure detaches both handlers and finishes the message stream, with no terminate call, and throws server(<the system error's description>). On success the connection is kept and its process is recorded with MCPHub.track so the app can end it at quit. Then: initialize with the connection's own first id, which is 1 on every launch (PR-MCP-237), and a 60-second timeout; a reply whose result is not an object throws server("The server sent something unexpected: missing result."); then the notifications/initialized notification is queued on the process's write queue; then initialized is set. Any failure in that block runs stop() and rethrows, wrapping errors that are neither MCPHubError nor CancellationError as server(<description>).
side_effects: launches a child process and records it in the live-process list
failure_cases: the two literal messages above, each ending with a full stop
records.cancellation: a cancellation during the handshake stops the client and rethrows CancellationError
records.windows_path: Same layering and cwd; stderr is buffered as the process does upstream and never shown by the hub. The live-process list must be wired to the app-quit path so no npx or node child survives the app; on Windows an orphan survives until Task Manager.
records.verification_method: integration test asserting no child survives app quit
records.b3_note: 1.7.0 launches through MCPStdioConnection: stderr is buffered instead of drained and discarded, a failed launch no longer calls terminate, initialize takes the connection's id 1 instead of the client's counter, and the notification is written on the process's write queue.

records.title: The hub's stdio requests share one connection that matches replies to requests by id, so two calls in flight do not steal each other's answers
source_evidence: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPHub.swift:243-264 stdioRPC and stdioReply - :253 let reply = try await connection.request(method, params, timeout: timeout) | :254 try checkReply(reply) | :259 throw MCPHubError.server(code.map { "The server quit (exit \($0))." } ?? "The server quit.") | :261 throw MCPHubError.server("The server didn't answer in time.")
DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:162-245 MCPStdioConnection's request, read, awaitReply, handle, abandon and close
records.action: A stdio request waits for its reply.
records.expected_result: Each request goes through MCPStdioConnection.request with the caller's timeout. The connection files every incoming message that is an object with an id under that id: a waiting request gets it at once, and any other is kept until a request for that id waits for it (PR-MCP-232), matching ids exactly (PR-MCP-233). A matched reply runs checkReply and is returned. When the child's exit is reported (PR-MCP-234) the request throws server("The server quit (exit <code>)."); the exit always carries a code, so the bare "The server quit." fallback at :259 is never reached. When the timer wins (PR-MCP-235) it throws server("The server didn't answer in time.") and the request's id is abandoned. There is no polling interval. Replies for other ids are KEPT, which is what lets two concurrent calls on one server each get their own.
failure_cases: the two literal messages above, each ending with a full stop
records.cancellation: a cancelled caller abandons the request's id and CancellationError propagates
records.windows_path: Event-driven matching with no polling interval, the same retention of replies for other ids, and exact id matching. The probe and the hub share this one reader.
records.verification_method: integration test issuing two concurrent calls to one stand-in server that answers them in reverse order
records.b3_note: 1.7.0 replaced waitStdio's 10 ms polling and replies map with MCPStdioConnection, which the probe shares; an exit is reported only after stdout ends or 1 s after the child exits, always with a code, and a string id no longer matches.

records.title: A hub HTTP client initializes once per client and never clears that flag except on stop
records.expected_result: An unparseable url throws server("The server address is invalid."). When not yet initialized: POST initialize with a 60-second timeout; an empty body throws server("The server sent something unexpected: empty reply."); an error reply throws through checkReply; a non-object result throws server("The server sent something unexpected: missing result."); the session id is adopted when present; initialized is set; then the notifications/initialized notification is posted with a 30-second timeout and its errors are swallowed EXCEPT CancellationError. Then the real request is posted with the caller's timeout; an empty body throws the empty-reply message; an error reply throws; the body is returned. There is no restart and no dead state on this path, and initialized is cleared only by stop(), so a client whose remote session was dropped keeps believing it is initialized until exportAll triggers a reload.
failure_cases: the four literal messages above
records.cancellation: each POST is a cancellation point
records.windows_path: Reproduce: do not clear initialized anywhere but stop, and add no restart to the HTTP path.
records.verification_method: integration test dropping the remote session and asserting the client does not re-initialize

records.title: The hub's HTTP POST sets the same four headers as the probe and reports a non-2xx by status alone
source_evidence: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPHub.swift:343-352 post - :345 return try await MCPWire.post(to: url, headers: headers, sessionID: sessionID, payload: payload, id: id, timeout: timeout) | :348 throw MCPHubError.server("The server sent something unexpected: invalid reply.") | :350 throw MCPHubError.server("The server answered \(status).")
DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPHub.swift:317, :328 and :335 the ids passed: the initialize id, nil for the notification, the request id
records.expected_result: The spec's headers are applied first, then Content-Type: application/json, Accept: application/json, text/event-stream and MCP-Protocol-Version: 2025-06-18, then Mcp-Session-Id when one is held. The timeout is the caller's. The JSON-RPC id of the payload is passed along (nil for the notification). A non-HTTP response throws server("The server sent something unexpected: invalid reply."). A status outside 200..<300 throws server("The server answered <status>.") - up to 2000 bytes of the body are read but NOT shown, unlike the probe, which carries them. The response Mcp-Session-Id is returned. A text/event-stream content type yields the frame whose id equals the request's, read as it arrives, or nil without reading for the notification (PR-MCP-117); otherwise the whole body is read, empty data yields nil, and anything else is parsed as JSON.
failure_cases: the two literal messages above
records.cancellation: the request is a cancellation point
records.windows_path: Same headers; the body omission on failure is a deliberate difference from the probe.
records.verification_method: contract fixture asserting the headers, the failure message, an event-stream reply whose matching frame follows a frame for another id, and a notification answered as a held-open event stream

deviation.upstream: Upstream sets the server's headers on the request and leaves redirects to URLSession, with no redirect delegate anywhere in the tree: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:66-72 - :66 for (field, value) in headers { request.setValue(value, forHTTPHeaderField: field) } | :72 let (bytes, response) = try await URLSession.shared.bytes(for: request)
deviation.port: nth sends a server's custom headers only to that server: a redirect that changes scheme, host or port drops them, and a same-server redirect keeps them. Authorization follows the same rule (ED-152).

records.b3_note: 1.7.0 made the hub's post a wrapper over MCPWire.post, which streams event-stream replies, matches the request id, and returns nil for a notification without reading.

records.title: The hub's tools/list request has a 60-second deadline
source_evidence: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPHub.swift:182 - try await self.rpc(method: "tools/list", params: params, timeout: 60), the page closure handed to MCPWire.listTools, whose up-to-ten-page loop is DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:41

porting/extracts/mcp-protocol-and-oauth.md:284-313 section 1.9 'Timeouts and intervals, exact numbers' - the full table of the area's eighteen deadlines. Its row for this call and the one for tools/call cite MCPHub.swift:201 and :238; the real call sites are :182 and :207 at B3, so trust the source lines given here
records.preconditions: A hub client is listing a server's tools.
records.expected_result: 60 seconds, per REQUEST and therefore per page: a listing that walks ten cursor pages may take up to 600 seconds in total, because the deadline is not shared across the loop. records.title: Stopping a hub client stops its stdio connection and forgets its session
source_evidence: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPHub.swift:173-178 stop() - :174 stdio?.stop() | :175 stdio = nil | :176 initialized = false | :177 sessionID = nil
records.action: stop() runs from reload, from a listing failure, or from a failed handshake.
records.expected_result: The stdio connection, when there is one, is stopped: its stdin is closed, the child is sent the terminate signal and, if it is still running 3 seconds later, killed by pid alone (PR-MCP-111). Then the connection reference, the initialized flag and the session id are cleared. Nothing else is cleared: the dead flag and the restart flag stay set, so a client that exhausted its restart stays dead until reload replaces it, and the http id counter keeps counting.
side_effects: closes the child's stdin, terminates and possibly kills the child process
failure_cases: none
records.windows_path: Same field set cleared and the same two flags deliberately left set; the child is stopped as PR-MCP-111 says.
records.verification_method: unit asserting the flags after stop
records.b3_note: 1.7.0 stop() only stops the MCPStdioConnection (stdin close, SIGTERM, pid-only SIGKILL after 3 s) and clears stdio, initialized and sessionID; B2 also detached the pipe handlers, cleared the conversation, stdin handle and replies map, and killed the process group after 1 s.

records.title: Every server process started this run is terminated when the app quits
source_evidence: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPHub.swift:355-376 MCPLiveProcesses - :357 private final class MCPLiveProcesses: Sendable { | :358 private let state = Mutex<[StdioProcess]>([]) | :362 processes.removeAll { !$0.isRunning } | :363 processes.append(process) | :368 let running = state.withLock { $0.filter(\.isRunning) } | :369 for process in running { process.terminate() } | :370 // The app is quitting, so the delayed SIGKILL in terminate() never fires. | :373 kill(getpgid(pid) == pid ? -pid : pid, SIGKILL)
records.action: terminateAll runs from the application-will-terminate path.
records.expected_result: The live-process list drops already-exited entries whenever a new one is added. terminateAll takes the running processes under the lock, terminates each (StdioProcess.terminate, which also queues a stdin close and schedules a kill 3 seconds later that never runs at quit), then kills any that is still running - the whole process group when the child leads one, otherwise the single pid. It is synchronous and does nothing asynchronous, because nothing asynchronous would get to run at quit. Without it a child process outlives its parent and an npx server would keep running until the machine restarts.
side_effects: terminates and kills every in-app MCP child process
failure_cases: a process that ignores both is left running, which the source accepts
records.windows_path: Wire this to the app-quit path and kill the whole process tree, not just the immediate child: npx spawns node as a grandchild and a per-pid kill leaks it. This is the platform boundary - Windows has no process groups, so a job object or a tree kill is the equivalent.
records.verification_method: integration test quitting the app with two servers running and asserting no orphan remains
records.b2_change: Moved: B1 :531-553 -> B2 :535-557. MCPLiveProcesses changed from NSLock plus `[Process]` (`@unchecked Sendable`) to B2 :538 private let state = Mutex<[Process]>([]) and is Sendable. add still prunes exited processes before appending; terminateAll still snapshots the running ones under the lock, terminates each, then kills survivors.
records.b3_note: 1.7.0 tracks StdioProcess objects instead of Process; terminateAll still terminates each running child and immediately kills survivors by group or pid.

records.title: The JavaScript bridge is installed beside the app's data and rewritten only when its text changed
records.preconditions: A Pi or Command Code session is starting.
records.expected_result: The base is the user's Application Support directory, falling back to <home>/Library/Application Support. The directory is <base>/<app display name>/MCP, created with intermediate directories. The file is droppy-mcp-bridge.mjs. Its bytes are the bridge source encoded as UTF-8; it is written atomically ONLY when the file's current contents differ, so a new build's bridge replaces the old one and an unchanged one is not touched. The file's URL is returned.
side_effects: may create a directory and write one file
failure_cases: a directory or write failure throws to the caller, which is the session launch
records.windows_path: macOS writes to <Application Support>/<AppName>/MCP while the provider configs live in <Storage.root>/mcp; on a case-insensitive filesystem those collapse, so write droppy-mcp-bridge.mjs into %LOCALAPPDATA%\<AppName>\mcp\ and derive the base from the OS app-data root rather than the capture-aware storage root. Keep the write-only-if-changed check. The path handed to Pi and Command Code must be importable by Node: a bare drive-letter path fails in a dynamic import, so hand them a file:// URL. That is a genuine porting decision, not a parity break, since the macOS POSIX path works as is.
records.verification_method: integration test asserting the file is written once and not rewritten on an unchanged relaunch

records.title: The bridge connects each server with a 15-second cap, strictly one after another, and never kills a spawned child
source_evidence: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPBridgeSource.swift:16-17 PROTOCOL_VERSION, interpolated from DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:7 and so still "2025-06-18" in the emitted script, and CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS
records.expected_result: Server keys are iterated in object order with an await inside the loop, so connections are strictly sequential and N hung servers cost N times 15 seconds of host startup. A member is remote when it is an object whose "type" is "http" and whose "url" is a string, and local when it is an object whose "command" is a string; anything else is ignored. Each connection is raced against a 15000 ms timer that rejects with "timed out"; the timer is cleared either way. A failure prints "droppy mcp: skipping <server>: <message>" to standard error and moves on. There is NO kill, unref or signal anywhere in the file, so a server abandoned at the timeout keeps its spawned child alive for the whole lifetime of the Pi or Command Code host. This is upstream behavior and is reproduced.
side_effects: spawns one child process per local server, some of which are never reaped
one console line per skipped server
failure_cases: a hung server leaks its process and delays startup by 15 seconds
records.windows_path: Reproduce: the bridge .mjs must not kill children and must stay sequential. On Windows the leak is worse, since an orphaned npx or node child of a host process survives with no process-group kill to catch it. Record it as an upstream defect rather than fixing it inside shipped text.
records.verification_method: integration test with a hung stand-in server asserting the 15-second skip and the surviving child

records.title: The bridge speaks a deliberately different dialect from the two Swift clients
source_evidence: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPBridgeSource.swift:138 and :203 the clientInfo with no version
DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPBridgeSource.swift:154-158 postMessage's headers and lowercase session header
records.preconditions: The bridge is connecting a server.
records.expected_result: initialize params are {protocolVersion: "2025-06-18", capabilities: {}, clientInfo: {name: "nth"}} - NO version field. Remote requests send the entry's headers plus Content-Type: application/json and Accept: application/json, text/event-stream, and NO MCP-Protocol-Version header at all; the session header is the lowercase "mcp-session-id" on both send and read. An SSE frame is accepted when its data parses to an object having "result" OR "error" - not, as in the Swift clients, an "id" - and a data payload of "[DONE]" is skipped. A tool's description falls back to its own name when absent or empty, and its schema falls back to the literal {type: "object"} with no properties key. Result content maps a text item to its text and EVERY other item to the literal "[image]", joined with newlines; an isError result is returned as "Error: " plus that text or, when empty, "Error: tool failed"; a thrown error is returned as "Error: " plus its message rather than rejecting.
failure_cases: a tool failure is returned as an "Error: …" string, so the host sees a successful call with error text
records.windows_path: Copy the bridge text character for character, except that the clientInfo name is "nth" (OD-0012 F1), including the missing header, the version-less clientInfo, the lowercase session header, the result-or-error SSE rule and the "[image]" catch-all. Normalizing the three clients would change what remote servers see from Pi and Command Code.
records.verification_method: contract fixture capturing the bridge's wire traffic against a stub server

deviation.upstream: The bridge identifies itself as "Droppy Code": DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPBridgeSource.swift:138 and :203 - await request("initialize", { protocolVersion: PROTOCOL_VERSION, capabilities: {}, clientInfo: { name: "Droppy Code" } });

records.title: The bridge's stdio transport frames JSON lines, matches replies by id, and fails every pending call when the child dies
records.expected_result: The child is spawned with the host environment plus the entry's env, and stdio ["pipe", "pipe", "ignore"] - stderr is discarded at the pipe level. Ids start at 0 and increment. stdout is accumulated and split on "\n"; each non-empty line is parsed and, when its id is pending, resolves that call. Writes are JSON plus a newline; a write error removes the pending entry and rejects. A child error event, or its exit, fails every pending call with {error: {message: <text>}} and rejects the connection once. The handshake is initialize, then the notifications/initialized notification with an empty params object, then tools/list paged until nextCursor is falsy, with an empty params object on the first page. Tools are then wrapped with a call function bound to tools/call.
side_effects: spawns a child process that is never killed
failure_cases: "process exited" is the message when the child dies
records.windows_path: Shipped JavaScript: copy verbatim. Note the spawn call passes a bare command name, which on Windows requires shell resolution for .cmd shims such as npx - that is a real platform boundary in text that must otherwise stay byte-identical, and it must be escalated rather than silently edited.
records.verification_method: integration test against a scripted stdio stand-in server

records.title: The bridge's remote transport carries a session id forward and swallows notification failures
records.expected_result: Ids start at 0 and increment. Each request posts JSON and adopts the response's mcp-session-id header, keeping the previous one when the response has none. A response with no usable message throws "empty response (status <status>)". An error member in the reply throws its message or "request failed". The notification helper posts and swallows every failure inside a bare try/catch. The handshake is initialize, then notifications/initialized with an empty params object, then tools/list paged until nextCursor is falsy. Tools are wrapped with a call function bound to tools/call.
failure_cases: "empty response (status <status>)" and "request failed"
records.windows_path: Shipped JavaScript: copy verbatim.
records.verification_method: contract fixture against a stub remote server

records.title: A stdio reply that arrives before its request waits, or for an id nobody is waiting on, is kept by id for a later wait
source_evidence: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:125-131 the connection state - :127 var pending: [RPCID: CheckedContinuation<JSONValue, Error>] = [:] | :128 var buffered: [RPCID: JSONValue] = [:]

DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:219-228 handle - :220 guard let object = message.object, | :221 let rawID = object["id"], let id = RPCID(rawID) else { return } | :223 if let continuation = state.pending.removeValue(forKey: id) { return continuation } | :224 state.buffered[id] = message

DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:198-217 awaitReply - :203 if let value = state.buffered.removeValue(forKey: id) { return .success(value) } | :204 if state.closed { return .failure(MCPWireError.exited(state.exitStatus)) } | :205 state.pending[id] = continuation
DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:164-168 the counter only ever increases, so an id is never reused on a connection
records.preconditions: A stdio connection (the probe's, or a hub client's) is running.
records.action: A message arrives on the child's stdout.
records.expected_result: A message that is not a JSON object, has no "id", or whose id is neither a number nor a string (for example null) is ignored. Otherwise, when a request is waiting for that id it is handed the message at once and stops waiting. When none is, the message is kept under its id, replacing any message kept earlier for the same id, and the next wait for that id takes it at once without suspending, so a reply that arrives before its request has started waiting is not lost. A reply for an id whose request already gave up (timed out, failed or was cancelled) stays kept for the life of the connection, because ids are never reused. A kept reply is still handed to a wait that begins after the child's exit was reported.
side_effects: holds unclaimed replies in memory for the life of the connection
failure_cases: a server that answers ids nobody asked for grows the kept set for the life of the connection
records.cancellation: not cancellable; a waiting request that is cancelled gives up its slot (PR-MCP-235)
records.windows_path: Keep a pending map and a kept-reply map keyed by the exact id (PR-MCP-233) under one lock, check the kept map before registering a wait, and never drop an unclaimed reply.
records.verification_method: unit with a scripted server that answers before the request is awaited, answers an id nobody asked for, and answers a request after it timed out
records.b3_note: New in 1.7.0: MCPStdioConnection replaces the B2 polling readers; the probe's reader discarded replies for other ids, and the hub's kept them only under an integer id.

records.title: Stdio replies are matched to requests by exact id: an integer request is not answered by a string id, while a fractional number is truncated and matches
source_evidence: DroppyCode/Core/Support/JSONRPC.swift:3-14 RPCID - :9 case .int(let id): self = .int(id) | :10 case .double(let id): self = .int(Int(id)) | :11 case .string(let id): self = .string(id) | :12 default: return nil
DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:221 let rawID = object["id"], let id = RPCID(rawID) else { return }
DroppyCode/Core/Support/JSONValue.swift:26-45 init(foundation:) - a number the JSON parser reports as floating point becomes .double, any other number .int
records.preconditions: A stdio request with integer id N is waiting.
records.expected_result: Each request waits under RPCID.int(N). A reply's id is converted the same way: a JSON integer stays that integer, a number the JSON parser reads as floating point (for example 1.5) is truncated toward zero and so answers request 1, a JSON string stays a string, and any other id is ignored. A string id therefore never answers an integer request, even when it spells the same number: a reply with "id": "1" is kept under the string (PR-MCP-232) and request 1 waits until its timer ends it, giving "The server didn't answer in time." in the hub and the timeout outcome in the probe. Event-stream replies over HTTP are matched differently (PR-MCP-117).
failure_cases: a server that echoes ids as strings times out on every request
records.windows_path: Match on a tagged id (integer or string) exactly as RPCID does, including the truncation of a fractional number; do not coerce numeric strings.
records.verification_method: unit: replies with "id": "1" and "id": 1.5 against request 1
records.b3_note: New in 1.7.0: B2 read stdio reply ids through JSONValue.int, which also accepted a numeric string such as "1"; MCPStdioConnection matches RPCID exactly.

records.title: A stdio request fails with the child's exit status: at once when the child is not running, and for waiting requests once the child's output has ended
source_evidence: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:163 guard process.isRunning else { throw MCPWireError.exited(await process.waitForExit()) }
DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:189-196 read - :192 for await message in messages { self.handle(message) } | :193 let status = await self.process.waitForExit() | :194 self.close(status: status)

DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:235-245 close(status:) - :237 guard !state.closed else { return [] } | :244 for continuation in pending { continuation.resume(throwing: MCPWireError.exited(status)) }
DroppyCode/Core/Support/StdioProcess.swift:154-157 finishOutput and :168-183 didExit - :179 DispatchQueue.global().asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + 1) { [weak self] in | :181 self?.finishOutput()
records.preconditions: A stdio connection whose child may have exited.
records.action: A request is made, or the child exits while requests wait.
records.expected_result: A request made when the child is no longer running sends nothing and fails with exited(<status>) once the child's exit status is known. Otherwise waiting requests keep waiting until the connection's message stream ends, which happens when the child's stdout closes, or 1 second after the child exits when something else (such as a grandchild) still holds stdout open. Messages the child wrote before that are delivered first. The connection then waits for the exit status, marks itself closed and fails every waiting request with exited(<status>); a wait that begins after that fails the same way at once, unless a reply for its id is already kept (PR-MCP-232). The status is always present, so the hub's message is always "The server quit (exit <code>)." and the probe's is the exited form of PR-MCP-110.
failure_cases: a child that exits while a grandchild keeps its stdout open is reported 1 second after its exit
a request's own timer can end it first (PR-MCP-235)
records.windows_path: Report the exit only after the output stream has ended (EOF, or 1 second after exit), always with the exit code, and fail every waiting request with it.
records.verification_method: integration test with a stand-in server that exits mid-request, one that exits while a child process keeps its stdout open, and a request made after the exit
records.b3_note: New in 1.7.0: the B2 polling loops noticed an exit on their next poll (the hub said a bare "The server quit." when the process was gone before its code was recorded); MCPStdioConnection waits for the output to end and always reports the status.

records.title: Each stdio request races its reply against a timer of its timeout, and a request that ends without a reply gives up its id
source_evidence: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPWire.swift:162-187 request - :170 return try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: JSONValue.self) { group in | :171 group.addTask { try await self.awaitReply(key) } | :173 try await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(timeout)) | :174 throw MCPWireError.timedOut | :176 self.process.send(MCPWire.request(id: id, method: method, params: params)) | :179 group.cancelAll() | :182 group.cancelAll() | :183 self.abandon(key)
records.preconditions: A stdio request was made on a running child.
records.expected_result: The request takes the connection's next id, starts a wait for that id and a timer of `timeout` seconds side by side, and only then queues the request line for the child's stdin. Whichever finishes first decides: a reply is returned and the timer is cancelled; the timer ending throws timedOut; an exit report throws exited(<status>) (PR-MCP-234). On any failure the other task is cancelled and the id is abandoned: its wait slot is removed and resumed with CancellationError, so nothing is left waiting. A cancelled caller cancels both tasks, the wait gives up its slot the same way, and CancellationError reaches the caller. A reply that comes after its request gave up is kept, not delivered (PR-MCP-232). The timer is per request: each hub call gets its own full timeout, and the probe hands in the time left before its deadline (PR-MCP-109).
side_effects: queues one JSON line for the child's stdin on the process's write queue
failure_cases: "The server didn't answer in time." in both callers when the timer wins
records.cancellation: cancelling the caller abandons the id and throws CancellationError
records.windows_path: Race the reply against a per-request timer; on timeout, error or cancellation remove the pending entry so that a late reply is only kept, and let CancellationError reach the caller.
records.verification_method: unit with a scripted server that never answers, one that answers after the timeout (kept, not delivered), and a caller cancelled mid-wait
records.b3_note: New in 1.7.0: B2 polled against a deadline every 10 ms (hub) or 5 ms (probe); MCPStdioConnection races a continuation against Task.sleep and abandons the id on failure.

records.title: A stdio connection's error tail is the last 4000 bytes its child wrote to stderr

records.preconditions: A stdio connection's child has written to stderr.

deviation.upstream: Upstream discards every deletion result and disconnect carries on as a success: DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPKeychain.swift:21-23 - :22 APIKeychain.delete(account(server: server, field: field)); DroppyCode/Services/Providers/APIKeychain.swift:76-83 - :82 SecItemDelete(query as CFDictionary); DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPStore.swift:118-120 - :118 MCPKeychain.deleteAll(server: entry) | :119 if entry.isOAuth { | :120 MCPOAuth.signOut(serverID: entry.id); DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPOAuth.swift:189-191 - :190 MCPKeychain.delete(server: serverID, field: "oauth") | :191 MCPKeychain.delete(server: serverID, field: "oauth-client"); upstream reports nothing, so it has no wording for the report
deviation.port: nth checks each credential deletion that disconnect makes and reports a failed one to the user instead of success (BLK-0012 ruling: "a failed credential deletion on disconnect is reported to the user instead of success"). Three details are ENGINEERING DECISIONS, not ruling text: the two OAuth items signOut deletes during disconnect (MCPStore.swift:119-120) are included, because they are credential deletions made on disconnect, although BLK-0012's quarantined sub-path names only deleteAll; an item that did not exist is not a failure, because upstream routinely deletes items that were never written (deleteAll walks every declared field whether set or not, and signOut deletes both OAuth items whether present or not); and the rest of disconnect still runs, because upstream's disconnect has no early exit (MCPStore.swift:115-128) and the ruling changes only what is reported. The report reads, per OD-0012 E6: "Disconnected, but Credential Manager did not remove this server’s stored values." Where it is shown is not given by the source or by the ruling (open_question).

records.open_question: OD-0012 E6 gives the text of the failed-deletion report ("Disconnected, but Credential Manager did not remove this server’s stored values.") but neither the ruling nor the source says where it is shown or for how long.

deviation.port: nth checks each credential deletion that disconnect makes and reports a failed one to the user instead of success (BLK-0012 ruling: "a failed credential deletion on disconnect is reported to the user instead of success"). Three details are ENGINEERING DECISIONS, not ruling text: the two OAuth items signOut deletes during disconnect (MCPStore.swift:119-120) are included, because they are credential deletions made on disconnect, although BLK-0012's quarantined sub-path names only deleteAll; an item that did not exist is not a failure, because upstream routinely deletes items that were never written (deleteAll walks every declared field whether set or not, and signOut deletes both OAuth items whether present or not); and the rest of disconnect still runs, because upstream's disconnect has no early exit (MCPStore.swift:115-128) and the ruling changes only what is reported. The report reads, per OD-0012 E6: "Disconnected, but Credential Manager did not remove this server’s stored values." Where it is shown is not given by the source or by the ruling (open_question).

records.open_question: OD-0012 E6 gives the text of the failed-deletion report ("Disconnected, but Credential Manager did not remove this server’s stored values.") but neither the ruling nor the source says where it is shown or for how long.

states: running: the breathing ring is drawn behind the glyph and does not take hit tests
failed: an xmark badge in the danger colour at the bottom trailing corner
declined: a hand.raised.slash badge in the warning colour
every other status: no badge
interactions: none; it is decoration on a tool call row
records.notes: exact_text is the accessibility label, built as the entry name plus a space and the word "tool". The badge transitions in with a combined scale and opacity. This is the only MCP element outside Settings.
